extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers in bibliometrics/scientometrics, citation analysis, and NLP (developers of citation classifiers)
extracted.subtask_description: Classifying in-text citations by their function, polarity, importance, and relevance (for understanding influence and for automatic classification). Includes guidance on features, annotation schemes, and methodological considerations for manual and automated analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation is useful for showing concepts, definitions, or interpretations, or for substantiating a statement or an assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation contributes additional information, data, a point of comparison, a theoretical equation, or methodology. Results of the citing paper furnish a new interpretation/explanation of the data of the cited source, a methodology, or formulation of research problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of relevant literature that are influential, essential, basic; descriptions of other relevant work. The results of the citing paper prove, verify, or substantiate data or interpretation of the cited source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfunctory (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation that is casual, unusual, neutral, or made with reservations, or for ceremonial purposes. It is included as a note or with no clear indication of reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical background; citations are mentioned in the introduction or discussion as part of the history and the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtapositional (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional information that is supplementary or illustrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmative (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited source is positively evaluated, is of critical importance to results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negational (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited source is negatively evaluated: partial or total negation; citation is made with criticism and another treatment is proposed by author (aims of correction, discussion, or disclaimer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other functions (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions beyond the main categories, e.g., alerting readers to forthcoming work, anticipated value, or new research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signposting (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directs readers to other sources to (1) inform readers of other relevant and interesting papers, (2) encourage readers to read more about the argument, and (3) save space (similar to 'further reading').

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations used to justify the topic, methodology and claims of the citing paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations made to pay respect and acknowledge others' ideas, findings, methods, etc. (including self-defense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Position (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations used to draw attention toward different viewpoints, clarify cited authors’ perspectives in detail, and show development of perspectives over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited work is criticized in a mild or harsh way (engagement/dispute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Building (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods or ideas of the cited document are used and developed further by the citing author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tying (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations that associate the citing authors with other researchers’ methodological approaches, schools of thought, paradigms, and disputes on specific scientific topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Used to make readers aware of the earlier works of the citing author or other researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations that point out the citing authors’ future research plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations used to show the citing author’s knowledge of the main literature in the discipline and their ability to conduct research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical (Harwood, 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations employed to show that the citing authors and their studies are concerned with the newest and most important topics in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential vs Perfunctory (Lin, 2018 / Moravcsik & Murugesan framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimension distinguishing citations that are essential (central to the citing work: conceptual, factual, methodology) versus perfunctory (incidental or ceremonial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in two-dimensional coding (crossed with confirmative/negational) to form compound categories such as 'essential-concept-confirmative' etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmative vs Negational (Lin, 2018 / Moravcsik & Murugesan framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimension distinguishing citations that confirm/support cited work (confirmative) versus those that criticize/refute it (negational).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often combined with essential/perfunctory to yield fine-grained categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation polarity (Teufel et al., 2006 et seq.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitude of the citing author toward the cited paper: positive (favorable), negative (unfavorable), or neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polarity helps assess the actual impact of cited works; mapping polarity to function can improve classification accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influential (important) vs Non-influential (perfunctory) classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary distinction labeling citations/papers as influential (useful/important to the citing work) versus non-influential/perfunctory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies report a small proportion of citations are influential (~10–14% in several studies); classifiers should target features that correlate with influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance levels (Ramos et al., 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-level relevance classification for cited works: 'great relevance' (cited main ideas), 'intermediate relevance' (cited techniques), 'minor relevance' (did not cite main ideas or techniques).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation frequency / recurring mentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of times a cited reference is mentioned in the citing document (recurrence within text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring citations with higher frequency are rated as more important; often used as a primary feature for 'influential' labeling (context-based feature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation length and depth of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of the citation context and how thoroughly the cited work is discussed (quoted/discussed multiple times vs barely mentioned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer, multiple-mention, or in-depth discussion correlates with higher citation importance; only a small percentage of references are thoroughly discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation location in the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Section of the citing paper where the citation appears (e.g., Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Related Work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations in Methods or cited multiple times are often considered more important; location is a strong predictor of function/importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-related features (known authors, self-citation, seniority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the cited author is known to the citer, whether author overlap/self-citation occurs, and seniority/ status of cited authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations whose authors were known to the citing author and self-citations for conceptual/method/data reasons tend to receive greater in-depth treatment; senior first authors also get more attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count-based features (Zhu et al., 2015)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative occurrence features such as number of times each reference appears in the citing document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful baseline features for classifiers; often combined with other feature types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity-based features
rubrics_metrics.description: Features measuring similarity (e.g., abstract similarity between cited and citing paper, title similarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies found abstract similarity helpful for detecting functions, others contrary — results are dataset-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-based / cue-word-based / text-based features
rubrics_metrics.description: Features derived from the textual citation context (lists of cue words to indicate related work, comparison, using/extending existing work) and text similarity between cited abstract and citing text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context-based and cue-word features are widely used to detect functions and importance; e.g., cue words help identify comparative or methodological citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position-based features
rubrics_metrics.description: Features about the position of citation within the paper beyond section (e.g., related work vs methods vs discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to prioritize citations in certain sections (methods often more important); should be combined with rhetorical/context features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous-based features
rubrics_metrics.description: Other features such as number of citations the cited paper has received, author overlap, or metadata-derived counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can supplement other features but may be noisy; used in some models for detecting influential papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine function, polarity, frequency, and location for best impact assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation that the best alternative to citation counts is to consider 'citation function', 'citation polarity', 'citation frequency' and 'citation location' together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jointly modeling these dimensions provides a more nuanced measure of scientific influence than raw counts alone (Hernández-Alvarez et al., 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Map citation polarity to function to improve classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological guidance to map polarity (positive/negative/neutral) into citation function modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies mapped polarity to function for more accurate classification (e.g., Hernández-Alvarez et al., 2017; Jha et al., 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization and clear annotation schemes for automated analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Need for clear, replicable operationalization (annotation schemes) that enable large-scale automated analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many previous studies lack clear operationalization; robust manual annotation and standardized categories are crucial for building reliable automatic classifiers (Bertin, Atanassova, Sugimoto, et al., 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity trade-off: general vs many fine-grained categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of whether to use a few general but exclusive functions (for comparability) versus many discipline-specific fine-grained categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General categories (e.g., background, methodological, comparison, negational, perfunctory) improve comparability across studies, but risk missing functions like topical, future, or conceptual; choice depends on goals and datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation and classifier validation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches used: manual annotation of a corpus, automatic labeling from training data, and defining features that achieve best classification results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies typically combine manual annotations with machine learning; adding/removing features can materially change classifier accuracy — cross-study comparisons are difficult without standardized schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey/interview methodological considerations (recall, fatigue, self-serving responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations of surveys and interviews: motivations may not be explicit in text; recall issues and memory limitations; fatigue; potential self-serving responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation: interview about recently published papers to reduce recall problems, keep interviews concise to avoid fatigue, and be aware responses may be biased (Willett, 2013; Harwood, 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical structure and citation location for better detection (NLP guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider rhetorical patterns/language and citation locations jointly when using NLP methods to identify citation functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account both rhetorical structure of citations and their location in text to improve automatic classification (Bertin, Atanassova, Sugimoto, et al., 2016).
